extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and TeX users who type mathematical papers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for typing mathematical formulas and displays in (plain) TeX: rules for line breaking, braces and delimiters, matrices, vertical spacing, display layout, and equation numbering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ties and ellipses in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ties (nonbreaking spaces, e.g. ~) and the proper ellipsis command in running text to prevent bad line breaks and to obtain correct spacing for sequences like lists of coefficients or indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain TeX allows you to write '\dots' in text as an abbreviation for '$\ldots\,$'. Use ties to prevent undesirable breaks between text and inline math (for example, avoid constructs that let a list or punctuation break onto a new line in the wrong place). Example: 'The coefficients $c_0$,~$c_1$, \dots,~$c_n$ are positive.' Exercise: identify what's bad about 'Clearly $a_i<b_i$ for~$i=1, 2, \ldots, n$'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where TeX may break math formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX will permit a line break in an inline formula only after a relation symbol (like =, <, →) or after a binary operation symbol (+, −, ×) when that symbol is at the formula's outer level (not inside braces or an \over).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commas never produce a break in math mode, so avoid putting commas inside $...$ where a break might be desirable. If you want to avoid breaks except after specific symbols, freeze subformulas with braces (e.g. '{x^2-y^2}') to make them unbreakable boxes. Only change such things when TeX actually breaks a formula badly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing or preventing breaks at specific points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use control sequences to permit or forbid breaking at a given point in a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To permit a break at an outer-level place use '\allowbreak'. A discretionary multiplication sign '\*' behaves like '\-' (allows break with dash penalty) but inserts a '×' rather than a hyphen. To prohibit a break, use penalties (e.g. '\penalty<number>') or the shortcut '\nobreak' which is '\penalty10000'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling break penalties: \relpenalty and \binoppenalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties control how willing TeX is to break after relation atoms or binary operation atoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain TeX sets '\relpenalty=500' and '\binoppenalty=700' by default. You can change these values globally or insert a specific '\penalty<number>' after an atom to override defaults in a particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Braces and set notation: correct delimiting and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '\{' and '\}' for literal braces and '\mid' for the vertical bar in set-builder notation; insert thin spaces inside braces around the condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '\{a,b,c\}', '\{\,x\mid x>5\,\}', or '\{\,x:x>5\,\}'. Some authors use ':' instead of '|'. Use thin spaces ('\,') inside the braces so the result looks natural in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimiter sizing with \bigl, \bigm, \bigr, \Big, \bigg, \Bigg
rubrics_metrics.description: When delimiters must grow with their contents, choose appropriate sizing macros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '\bigl', '\bigm' (for middle bars) and '\bigr' around expressions like '(x,f(x)\mid x\in D)' as in '\bigl\{\,\bigl(x,f(x)\bigr)\bigm|x\in D\,\bigr\}'. For still larger delimiters use '\Big' or '\bigg' variants as needed (see Chapter 17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long textual conditions inside set notation — avoid \hbox pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting long English conditions inside an \hbox in math mode prevents line breaks and can produce poor spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example problematic form: '\{\,p\mid\hbox{$p$ and $p+2$ are prime}\,\}'. Because an \hbox can't break across lines and its glue does not vary with the surrounding interword glue, you should instead alternate between math mode and horizontal mode so that line breaks can occur where sensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting piecewise definitions with \cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the '\cases' construction to typeset piecewise definitions or selections; '&' separates the math part (left) from the text part (right) and each case ends with '\cr'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The '\cases' macro provides its own left brace (no corresponding '}'). Left of '&' is implicitly in math mode; right of '&' is horizontal mode (text). Blank spaces after '&' are ignored. Use '\noalign{\vskip...}' just after a '\cr' if extra vertical spacing between cases is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using \overbrace and \underbrace
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '\overbrace' and '\underbrace' to put horizontal braces above or below parts of a displayed formula; they act like large operators and may take limits (superscripts/subscripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '$$\overbrace{x+\cdots+x}^{k\rm\;times}$$' and '$$\underbrace{x+y+z}_{>\,0}$$'. Treat them as operators similar to '\sum' for limit placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing matrices: \matrix, \pmatrix, alignment tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: Matrices are created with '\matrix' and related macros; entries are separated by '&' and rows terminated by '\cr'. You normally supply '\left' and '\right' delimiters (or use '\pmatrix' to get parentheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '$$A=\left(\matrix{x-\lambda&1&0\cr 0&x-\lambda&1\cr 0&0&x-\lambda\cr}\right).$$' Entries are centered by default, each column width fits its widest entry, and a quad separates columns. To flush right in a column prefix entry with '\hfill'; to flush left follow the entry with '\hfill'. Each entry is typeset as a separate math formula in text style, so local font changes (e.g. '\rm') do not affect other entries; don't attempt constructs like '{\rm x&y}'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses in matrices: \vdots, \ddots, \ldots
rubrics_metrics.description: When matrices are given as generic patterns, insert ellipses in their own rows or columns using the appropriate dot commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '\vdots' for vertical dots, '\ddots' for diagonal dots, and '\ldots' for horizontal ellipses. Example generic matrix specified with '\pmatrix' and rows containing '\vdots' and '\ddots'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bordered matrices with \bordermatrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '\bordermatrix' to typeset matrices that have labels on the top row and left column; the first row supplies upper labels, the first column supplies left labels, and the first column in the first row is usually blank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '$$M=\bordermatrix{&C&I&C'\cr C&1&0&0\cr I&b&1-b&0\cr C'&0&a&1-a\cr}$$'. '\bordermatrix' inserts its own parentheses like '\pmatrix'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small matrices and inline arrays
rubrics_metrics.description: Large matrix macros are not intended for very small inline arrays; use small-array constructions (e.g. '{1\,1\choose0\,1}') or other macros for compact inline matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The '\matrix' macro doesn't produce small arrays; for small inline patterns use constructs like '\choose' and '{a\atop b}' as demonstrated for compact matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical spacing control: \phantom, \vphantom, \hphantom, \smash, \mathstrut
rubrics_metrics.description: Use phantom and strut macros to affect the perceived width/height/depth of subformulas without printing content, and use '\smash' to zero out height/depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: '\phantom{...}' reserves the full width/height/depth but is invisible; '\vphantom{...}' reserves height and depth only (width zero); '\hphantom{...}' reserves width only (height/depth zero); '\smash{...}' makes height and depth zero. '\mathstrut' is an abbreviation for a vertical strut useful in aligning fractions and roots. Example: '\mathop{\smash\limsup\vphantom\liminf}' makes a large operator with the height/depth of '\liminf'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising and lowering boxes: \raise and \lower
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '\raise' and '\lower' to move boxes up or down in formulas; remember that '\raise' operates on boxes and an \hbox will normally be in text style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '$2^{\raise1pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle n$}}$' moves the superscript up by 1pt. When raising in superscripts you may need to specify '\scriptstyle' for correct sizing. These techniques are useful when '\root' or default placement is not suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing math layout parameters (fontdimen) with care
rubrics_metrics.description: You can globally adjust positions of subscripts/superscripts and other math layout parameters by changing font dimensions (\fontdimen<n>\tensy etc.), but these changes are global and must be used cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example for chemical typesetting: setting '\fontdimen16\tensy=2.7pt' and '\fontdimen17\tensy=2.7pt' lowers all normal subscripts to align plus signs in superscripts. There are many fontdimen parameters controlling axis line position, numerator/denominator positions, limit spacing, rule thickness, etc. See Appendix G for precise details. Avoid forcing users to type manual positioning macros if a global parameter change is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive math-mode controls: \nonscript, \everymath, \everydisplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '\nonscript' to omit glue/kern in script or scriptscript styles, and use '\everymath' or '\everydisplay' to prepend tokens automatically to every inline/display math formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the sequence '\nonscript\;' produces spacing equivalent to the '3' entry in the math spacing table when not in scripts. '\everymath={...}' is analogous to '\everypar' and can be used to enforce conventions for all inline math; '\everydisplay={...}' does likewise for displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a personal notebook and prefer clear notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Record non-obvious formulas and how you typed them for future reference; choose notation for clarity and avoid overly elaborate notation even when beautifully typeset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: keep a notebook showing final output and the code you typed to produce it, to refer back months later. Prefer notation that communicates to readers; treat written exposition as if you were speaking to a friend—use symbolism only when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing and text inside displays: use \hbox and spacing commands
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining text and formulas in displays, use '\hbox' for text and spacing primitives ('\quad', '\qquad') to indicate relationships between parts of the display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '$$X_n=X_k \qquad\hbox{if and only if}\qquad Y_n=Y_k \quad\hbox{and}\quad Z_n=Z_k.$$' For text with math inside the text, nest math inside an hbox: '\qquad\hbox{for all $n\ge0$.}' so that mode nesting mirrors the intended logical grouping and spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation numbering: use of \eqno and \leqno and formatting of numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach equation numbers with '\eqno' (right margin) or '\leqno' (left margin); the equation number must be given second and is typeset in text style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '$$x^2-y^2=(x+y)(x-y).\eqno(15)$$' or '$$x^2-y^2=(x+y)(x-y).\leqno(16)$$'. Right-hand numbering is often preferred because displays usually end sentences. You can get en-dashes in numbers, e.g. '(3--1)', because numbers are text formulas. Tricks: '\eqno\llap{...}' or '\leqno\rlap{...}' can make the apparent width zero and force special positioning or put the number on a line by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX's display layout algorithm and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX computes display placement using registers like \displaywidth, \displayindent, and \predisplaysize, then packages the display into a box and applies a 'squeeze routine' if it doesn't fit; centering interacts with the equation number width and with glue/penalty parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational details: when a display begins \prevgraf is noted and \displaywidth/\displayindent are set from the paragraph shape; \predisplaysize is set from the previous line width (or to -\maxdimen if no previous line). TeX converts the math list to a horizontal list h in display style; let w0 be its natural width and e the equation-number width (if any) and q=e+one quad. If w0+q ≤ z (displaywidth) it boxes naturally; otherwise TeX will attempt to shrink the formula to z-q if enough shrinkability exists, else it sets e=0 and boxes to min(w0,z). Centering is done without regard to the equation number but adjusted if the number would be too close (d = 1/2(z-w), reset if d<2e, etc.). Which vertical glue (\abovedisplayskip vs \abovedisplayshortskip) is used depends on whether the preceding line overlaps the display (comparison of d+s and p). Understanding these parameters lets you predict and control display placement and line/page breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control page breaks and display penalties: \predisplaypenalty and \postdisplaypenalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \predisplaypenalty and \postdisplaypenalty to discourage or encourage page breaks just before or after displays; plain TeX defaults \predisplaypenalty=10000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because fine printers usually avoid displays at the top of a page, plain TeX sets \predisplaypenalty=10000. To force a page break placing the formula at the bottom line, use something like '$$\postdisplaypenalty=-10000\dots$$' rather than an explicit '\eject', since \eject after a display leaves unwanted glue and makes the page short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcing an equation number onto its own line
rubrics_metrics.description: You can force an equation number onto a line by itself by giving it zero apparent width, which changes TeX's positioning logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the equation-number box have width zero by using '\llap' with '\eqno' or '\rlap' with '\leqno' (e.g. '\eqno\llap{$...$}'). This sets e=0 in TeX's algorithm and causes placement rules to treat the number separately, allowing it to appear on its own line if necessary.
